description: Five visitor-accessible rounds across Wisconsin: the Ryder Cup Straits course at Whistling Straits, the 2017 U.S. Open site Erin Hills, Mike Keiser's Sand Valley resort, the 1930 Langford & Moreau classic Lawsonia Links, and Pete Dye's Blackwolf Run River Course.
intro: Wisconsin has quietly built one of the strongest lineups of public-access golf in America — major-championship venues, Golden Age classics, and one of the country's best modern resorts all sit within a few hours of Milwaukee. Everything on this list is open to traveling golfers: public or resort courses you can book without a membership. Most visitors base around Kohler or Milwaukee and work outward; the five below cover lakeside links-style golf, Kettle Moraine parkland, Golden Age architecture, and resort golf done right.

sections.heading: 1. Whistling Straits — Straits Course, Haven
paragraphs: The Straits Course at Whistling Straits is the most famous round in Wisconsin and the rare major-championship venue an ordinary visitor can simply book. Designed by Pete Dye for Herb Kohler and opened in 1998 on the Lake Michigan shore at Haven, it was reshaped from a flat former army site with imported sand into around a thousand bunkers, grazing sheep, and nine holes running along the water. The championship pedigree is as deep as any public course in the country: three PGA Championships (2004, 2010, 2015), the 2007 U.S. Senior Open, and the 2021 Ryder Cup, where the United States won by a record 19–9.

Book this as your anchor round and plan around it first — tee times are easiest to secure by staying at a Destination Kohler property such as The American Club, and non-guests should call the reservation team rather than assuming online inventory will be there. The Straits is walking-only, so budget a caddie and bring a carry bag rather than a loaded cart bag; the wind off Lake Michigan is a real opponent on the exposed lakeside holes. If the Straits is full, its Pete Dye-designed sibling, the Irish Course, sits right next door and plays from the same booking system.

sections.heading: 2. Erin Hills, Erin
paragraphs: Erin Hills, about 35 miles northwest of Milwaukee in the Kettle Moraine region, brought the U.S. Open to Wisconsin for the first time when it hosted the 2017 championship, won by Brooks Koepka. The course opened in 2006 and was designed by the team of Dr. Michael Hurdzan, Dana Fry, and Ron Whitten on 652 acres of glacially sculpted terrain — kettle moraine topography with wetlands and fine fescue fairways. It is a daily-fee public facility that walked onto the major-championship stage while staying open to everyone, and it has also hosted the U.S. Women's Amateur Public Links and the 2011 U.S. Amateur.

Erin Hills is a walking-only course, so plan to carry or take a caddie, and advance reservations are required — walk-ins are not guaranteed. The fairways are famously generous and the challenge is mostly in the fescue rough, wind, and length, so it rewards golfers who miss it wide rather than short and crooked. It pairs beautifully with a Whistling Straits trip: about two hours separate the two properties, making an Erin Hills–Kohler four-day loop the classic Wisconsin golf itinerary.

sections.heading: 3. Sand Valley, Nekoosa
paragraphs: Sand Valley is Mike Keiser's Wisconsin answer to Bandon Dunes: a sprawling public golf resort built on central Wisconsin sand country, roughly 100 miles north of Madison. The resort opened its namesake course — designed by Bill Coore and Ben Crenshaw — in 2017, followed by David McLay Kidd's Mammoth Dunes in 2018, plus the 17-hole Coore-Crenshaw Sandbox par-3 course, Tom Doak's The Lido and Sedge Valley, making it a true multi-day destination. All courses are walking-only and open to visitors, and the architecture-heavy, fun-first philosophy has made it one of the hottest tickets in travel golf.

This is the trip to take with a group, and lodging books up far in advance — plan group bookings well ahead, since on-property rooms are the scarce resource. The golf is golf-first and walking-first: carry, use a pushcart, or take a caddie, and build days around 36 holes with an evening session on The Sandbox. Mix the original Sand Valley, the most demanding of the layouts, with the friendlier, enormous fairways of Mammoth Dunes so the week has both a test and a joy round.

sections.heading: 4. Lawsonia Links, Green Lake
paragraphs: The Links Course at the Golf Courses of Lawsonia is one of the great Golden Age public courses in America. Built in 1930 by William Langford and Theodore Moreau on the farmland of Victor Lawson, it remains virtually unchanged from the day it opened — deep bunkers, wide fairways, and some of the wildest green complexes in the Midwest, including the famous par-3 seventh, the Box Car Hole. It sits on the top-100 public lists of every major golf magazine and offers two championship 18-hole layouts, the Links and the Woodlands, both open to visitors.

Lawsonia is the value anchor of this list: world-class architecture at an everyday public-course booking, with a season running roughly April through November. The greens are the story — favor below-the-hole positions and play the short game conservatively your first time through. It sits in Green Lake, about an hour northwest of Milwaukee and on the way to Sand Valley, so it slots naturally between a Milwaukee-base day and the Nekoosa trip; golf packages are available through on-property houses or the nearby Heidel House Resort.

sources.title: Lawsonia Links is a true classic in Wisconsin — GolfPass

sections.heading: 5. Blackwolf Run — River Course, Kohler
paragraphs: The River Course at Blackwolf Run completes the Destination Kohler major-championship story and may be Pete Dye's most penal public design. Opened in 1988 on the family land behind the Kohler factory and named that year's Best New Public Course by Golf Digest, it is woven through a glacial river basin with the meandering Sheboygan River coming into play on 10 of the 18 holes. The composite original course hosted the 1998 and 2012 U.S. Women's Opens — Se Ri Pak won in 1998 — along with the Andersen Consulting World Golf Championships in the mid-1990s.

This is the round to pair with Whistling Straits on a Kohler trip: both book through the same Destination Kohler system, and the two courses offer completely different Pete Dye tests — one lakeside links-style, one inland river-basin. The River Course is famously difficult, so play an honest tee and save aggressive lines for Meadow Valleys if you add the second Blackwolf Run 18. Staying at The American Club simplifies the booking window, and with Sheboygan River water lurking everywhere, bring more balls than your ego thinks you'll need.
